temptingClaims: A grain's velocity can be read off its path under the microscope.
whyTempting: A path is a record of positions in time, and a velocity is a distance divided by a time, so it seems enough to time a grain between two positions.
whereItIsTrue: For a motion that is smooth on the scale of the observation, a distance divided by a time does estimate a speed. The motion of a suspended grain is not smooth on any interval the paper considers.

whatIsTrue.r0: The distance a grain covers grows as the square root of the time, so a distance divided by a time depends on how often you look. The paper works with the displacement in a stated time, not with a velocity.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 4 introduces a time interval \(\tau\), very small against the intervals one can observe but long enough that a grain's motions in two successive intervals are independent (p. 556). From there it finds the mean displacement along an axis, \(\lambda_x = \sqrt{2Dt}\), and remarks that the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time (p. 559). Divided by the time, it gives \(\sqrt{2D/t}\), which grows as the interval shrinks. BM-01's velocity trap shows it: at the default settings the apparent speed is 0.79 μm/s for an interval of one second and 1.59 μm/s for a quarter of a second, twice as large for a quarter of the time.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) § 4: successive intervals carry independent motions, so the mean square of the displacement adds up interval by interval and grows in proportion to the time, \(\lambda_x^2 = 2Dt\). (2) The typical distance is its square root, \(\lambda_x = \sqrt{2Dt}\). (3) An apparent speed is that distance divided by the time: \(\lambda_x/t = \sqrt{2D}/\sqrt{t}\). (4) A quarter of the interval doubles the apparent speed, and a hundredth multiplies it by ten. (5) The number records the observer's choice of interval, not a property of the grain, which is why the paper's observable is the displacement in a stated time.
whatIsTrue.r3: The paper never reports a velocity for a suspended grain; its numbers are displacements, 0.8 micron in one second and about 6 microns in one minute (p. 559). BM-01 lets a reader choose the apparent speed as its statistic and change the interval to watch the number move.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 549–560 (1905), plates pp. 556 and 559
